input: The two groups report lifetime values that are quite different from one another, and it is instructive to consider how far the difference can be explained by the conditions under which the tests were carried out. In the first group's work, the benchmark material was aged under a humid feed of working composition, with regeneration steps between the periods of exposure, whereas the second group stored the material under a dry inert atmosphere and assessed the loss of performance only when it was returned to service. The first of these protocols subjects the benchmark material to essentially the stress it would experience in service, water taken up into the pores and driven out again in each cycle, while the second protocol removes this stress altogether and effectively measures storage stability rather than working life. It follows that a lifetime obtained from the second protocol is best regarded as an upper bound on the working lifetime rather than as an estimate of it, and the difference between the two reported values gives an indication of the magnitude of the cycling effect under the conditions used by the first group. On balance, the value obtained from the cycling protocol is preferred here as the basis for design purposes. This preference is, however, a limited one, since it depends on the service in question actually cycling the material through wetting and regeneration in the manner of the first protocol; where the service instead involves steady dry duty, the storage protocol is the more appropriate comparison and its value should be used. It is also worth noting that the IAST ranking of the fresh material offers no help in choosing between the two values, since both groups recorded the same fresh capacity before the ageing treatments began, and how the cycling value changes when the feed contains working-stream contaminants remains open.
target: The lifetime values reported for the benchmark material differ between the two groups, and the difference follows the test conditions more closely than it follows the material. One group aged the benchmark material under a humid feed at working composition, with regeneration between exposures; the other held the material under a dry inert atmosphere and measured the loss of performance on return to service. The first protocol loads the material with the stress that service applies, namely water carried into the pores and driven out again at each cycle. The second removes that stress and substitutes storage stability for working life. A lifetime from the second protocol is therefore an upper bound on the working lifetime, not an estimate of it, and the gap between the two values is the size of the cycling effect under the conditions of the first protocol. On that reading, the preference here is for the value from the cycling protocol, as the basis for design. The preference is limited: it rests on the service in question cycling the material through wetting and regeneration, as the first protocol does. Where service instead holds the material under steady dry duty, the storage protocol is the closer match and its value governs. The IAST ranking of the fresh material does not discriminate between the two values, because both groups measured the same fresh capacity before ageing began. What remains open is the rate at which the cycling value itself falls once the feed carries the contaminants of a working stream, which neither protocol admits, and the comparison stands unresolved on that point.
